title: Up the hill, weeping (2 Samuel 15:30)
hook: the fleeing king climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered
carry: he let the hard day be hard

segments.voice: Yesterday Absalom stole the lev, the heart, of everyone at the gate. Your line was a kiss, a nod, a sigh. Today, those stolen hearts become a revolt, and his father leaves the city on foot.

A messenger runs into the palace with one sentence: the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom. Absalom has had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, and he's coming. David doesn't try to hold the city. Arise, he says, let us flee, or none of us will escape him. So the king of Israel walks out of his own city, his household behind him, crosses the brook Kidron, and starts up the slope on the far side. Not riding. Walking. Barefoot.
screen: `THE HEARTS ARE AFTER ABSALOM.` → `ARISE, LET US FLEE.` → `ACROSS THE KIDRON, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: The verse is a slow picture. David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and "wept as he went up". His head was covered. He went barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads too, and went up weeping. Some readers see a mourner in the covered head and bare feet. The king who once danced before the ark with all his might now climbs a hill like a mourner. In Hebrew the verse keeps saying the same two things: going up, weeping, one step at a time. What's striking is what David does on the way. He doesn't give up. He sends the priests back to the city with the ark: if I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, God will bring me back and let me see it again. And if not, here I am; let God do to me what seems good. Then he hears that Ahithophel, his own wise counselor, has joined Absalom, and he prays a short, practical prayer: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. At the top, where God was worshipped, a loyal friend named Hushai is waiting, his coat torn and earth on his head, and David gives him a job. So the climb is two things at once. It is grief, honest and out loud, in front of everyone. And it is still movement. Weeping didn't stop David walking, and walking didn't stop him weeping.
screen: `HEAD COVERED. BAREFOOT.` · then, large: `UP THE HILL, WEEPING.` · then: `IF I FIND FAVOR, HE WILL BRING ME BACK.` · `A FRIEND WAITS AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: If your feet are free, press them flat on the floor and feel the ground, the way a barefoot walker would. Bring to mind something heavy you're carrying, and without fixing it or pretending it's light, name it, then name the next small step: one email, one call, one meal. If you pray, you can say David's words: here I am.
Barefoot. How David climbed the Mount of Olives after fleeing Jerusalem, head covered, grieving, still moving forward. Today's word.
Your line: he let the hard day be hard. And he kept going up the hill. More tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read David's flight from Jerusalem as part of the book of Samuel; the heading of Psalm 3 links that psalm to the time David fled from Absalom his son.

chat.says: Why does the Bible show King David crying in front of everyone as he fled?
options: He grieved openly, yet kept moving: sending the ark back, praying, planning.
He had given up, and the weeping shows he planned to surrender.
He was pretending, so Absalom's spies would think he was beaten.
chat.meaning: David went up weeping, head covered and barefoot, yet still sent the ark back, prayed, and gave Hushai a job.

Kidron.meaning: the brook David crossed as he left Jerusalem

Mount of Olives.meaning: the hill David climbed, weeping, after crossing the Kidron

Ahithophel.meaning: David's wise counselor, who joined Absalom

Hushai.meaning: David's loyal friend, waiting at the top

Hebron.meaning: where Absalom had himself proclaimed king
